```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(ggthemes)

slides_theme = theme_minimal(
  base_family = "Atkinson Hyperlegible",
  base_size = 16)

theme_set(slides_theme)

set.seed(220)

reviews <- read_csv("https://stat220-f26.github.io/data/en_coursera_sample.csv")

bigram_probs <- reviews |>
  unnest_tokens(output = bigram, input = Review, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  filter(!is.na(bigram)) |>
  separate(bigram, into = c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") |>
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE) |>
  group_by(word1) |>
  mutate(prob = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

generate_text <- function(start, n_words = 10) {
  words <- start
  for (i in seq_len(n_words)) {
    next_word <- bigram_probs |>
      filter(word1 == words[length(words)]) |>
      slice_sample(n = 1, weight_by = prob) |>
      pull(word2)
    if (length(next_word) == 0) break
    words <- c(words, next_word)
  }
  paste(words, collapse = " ")
}
```

## Today {.nonincremental}

1. What you built
2. Where it breaks
3. What LLMs change
4. Takeaways

## Autocomplete {.center}

When you type a text message, your phone suggests the next word.

. . .

Today's question: **what would it take to turn your bigram model into something like ChatGPT?**

# What you built {.maize}

## A language model

::: {.nonincremental}
A *language model* assigns a probability to the next token, given the text so far.
:::

1. Split text into tokens (here: words)
2. Count which tokens follow which
3. Turn counts into probabilities
4. *Sample* the next token, and repeat

## From counts to probabilities

```{r}
#| echo: true
bigram_probs |>
  filter(word1 == "great") |>
  slice_max(prob, n = 5)
```

## Sampling the next word

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
bigram_probs |>
  filter(word1 == "great") |>
  slice_sample(n = 1, weight_by = prob) |>
  pull(word2)
```

. . .

Always picking the most likely word gives the same boring text every time. Sampling gives different text each run, with likely words chosen more often.

## Text from your model

```{r}
#| echo: true
generate_text("this", n_words = 12)
generate_text("the", n_words = 12)
generate_text("i", n_words = 12)
```

# Where it breaks {.maize}

## Problem 1: one word of context

Each new word only "sees" the word right before it, so sentences wander.

```{r}
#| echo: false
generate_text("great", n_words = 15)
```

. . .

Nothing connects the beginning of a sentence to its end.

## Problem 2: words it has never seen

```{r}
#| echo: true
generate_text("xyzzy", n_words = 10)
```

. . .

If a word never appeared in the training reviews, the model has nothing to say.

## Problem 3: no notion of meaning

To the model, `great` and `excellent` are just two unrelated rows in a table. What it learns about one tells it nothing about the other.

```{r}
#| echo: false
bigram_probs |>
  filter(word1 %in% c("great", "excellent", "awesome", "fantastic", "superb", "terrific")) |>
  group_by(word1) |>
  summarize(`times seen` = sum(n), `different next words` = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(`times seen`))
```

. . .

Words that mean almost the same thing end up with very different amounts of data.

## Problem 4: more context means less data

```{r}
#| echo: false
tri_counts <- reviews |>
  unnest_tokens(output = trigram, input = Review, token = "ngrams", n = 3) |>
  filter(!is.na(trigram)) |>
  count(trigram)

bi_counts <- bigram_probs

tibble(
  model = c("Bigrams (1 word of context)", "Trigrams (2 words of context)"),
  `different combinations` = scales::comma(c(nrow(bi_counts), nrow(tri_counts))),
  `seen only once` = scales::percent(c(mean(bi_counts$n == 1), mean(tri_counts$n == 1)), accuracy = 1)
)
```

. . .

Looking at more words makes the model smarter, but most combinations are then ones it has barely seen.

# What LLMs change {.maize}

## Fix 1: tokens are pieces of words

LLMs usually split text into *subword tokens*, not words. Rare and new words are built from familiar pieces.

```
unbelievably helpful instructors

un | believ | ably |  helpful |  instruct | ors
```

::: {.aside}
Illustrative only. Real tokenizers split text differently.
:::

## Fix 2: meaning as numbers

Each token is represented by a list of numbers (an *embedding*), learned so that tokens used in similar contexts get similar numbers.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "A scatterplot with made-up two-dimensional coordinates for words. Great, excellent, and fantastic are close together, python, java, and code are close together, and instructor, teacher, and professor are close together."
emb <- tribble(
  ~word,        ~x,   ~y,
  "great",      1.0,  3.2,
  "excellent",  1.4,  3.5,
  "fantastic",  0.8,  3.7,
  "boring",     1.2,  0.6,
  "terrible",   0.7,  0.9,
  "python",     4.2,  2.1,
  "java",       4.6,  2.4,
  "code",       4.0,  2.7,
  "instructor", 2.6,  1.2,
  "teacher",    2.9,  1.5,
  "professor",  2.4,  1.6
)

ggplot(emb, aes(x, y, label = word)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.8, size = 5) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = "Made-up coordinates, for illustration") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

. . .

This lets a model handle contexts it has never seen *exactly*.

## Fix 3: attention

Instead of one previous word, the model looks at all of the text so far and learns which earlier words matter most for the next one.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: "A sentence 'the instructors were so helpful that I' with arrows from the next-word position pointing to earlier words. The thickest arrows point to 'instructors' and 'helpful'."
w <- c("the", "instructors", "were", "so", "helpful", "that", "I", "...?")
att <- tibble(
  word = w[1:7],
  x = 1:7,
  weight = c(0.3, 2.2, 0.4, 0.4, 2.8, 0.8, 1.0)
)

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = att,
    aes(x = 8, xend = x, y = 1, yend = 0.15, linewidth = weight),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.12, "inches")),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_text(data = tibble(x = 1:8, y = 0, word = w), aes(x, y, label = word), size = 6) +
  scale_linewidth(range = c(0.2, 2.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.2, 1.2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = "Made-up weights, for illustration") +
  theme_void(base_family = "Atkinson Hyperlegible")
```

. . .

This idea, plus a very large neural network, is what a *transformer* is.

## Training at scale

::: {.nonincremental}
Same task as your bigram model: **predict the next token**.
:::

1. *Pretraining*: predict the next token over a huge amount of text, with an enormous number of adjustable numbers
2. *Fine-tuning*: further training, including human feedback, so the model follows instructions and is helpful

## Temperature

Temperature controls how much the model favors the top choices when it samples.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "Three bar charts of next-word probabilities after 'great'. At low temperature, 'course' has nearly all the probability. At high temperature, the probabilities are spread more evenly across words."
great_next <- bigram_probs |>
  filter(word1 == "great")

crossing(temp = c(0.5, 1, 2), great_next) |>
  group_by(temp) |>
  mutate(p_adj = prob^(1 / temp) / sum(prob^(1 / temp))) |>
  slice_max(prob, n = 8) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(temp = factor(temp, labels = c("Low (0.5)", "Medium (1)", "High (2)"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = p_adj, y = fct_reorder(word2, prob))) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~temp) +
  labs(x = "Probability of next word, after \"great\"", y = NULL)
```

# Takeaways {.maize}

## Three things to remember

1. An LLM is the same idea you built: predict the next token, then sample. What changes is how much context it uses and how words are represented.
2. It predicts *plausible* text, not *true* text, so a fluent answer can be wrong.
3. Its outputs reflect its training data (Step 6 of the activity).
